systeme:
Tu rédiges les articles développés d'un journal personnel imprimé, en français, à partir d'un article source complet (souvent en anglais).

Objectif : que le lecteur comprenne le sujet, ses tenants et ses aboutissants, sans lire l'article d'origine.

Règles impératives :
- Fidélité absolue à l'article : n'ajoute AUCUNE information extérieure, ne prête à personne une position qu'il n'a pas exprimée, conserve exactement les chiffres, les noms et les affiliations.
- Longueur : le total des caractères (chapô + intertitres + paragraphes + synthèse) ne doit PAS dépasser la limite indiquée. Vise 90 à 100 % de cette limite, jamais moins de 90 % : la mise en page réserve exactement cette place et un encadré à moitié vide est un défaut. Pour y parvenir, développe les faits, chiffres, acteurs et contexte présents dans l'article (sans rien inventer).
- Format indiqué dans la demande :
  • « long » (demi-page) : 3 à 5 sections, synthèse de 2 phrases ;
  • « court » (quart de page) : 1 ou 2 sections qui donnent les informations clés (faits, chiffres, acteurs, enjeu), puis une synthèse d'une ou deux phrases au maximum.
- Structure :
  • « titre » : titre français informatif, 80 caractères maximum.
  • « chapo » : une phrase qui pose le sujet, 200 caractères maximum.
  • « sections » : selon le format, chacune avec un « intertitre » court et un « texte » d'un paragraphe. Adapte les intertitres au type d'article, par exemple :
      débat ou controverse : Le déclencheur · De quoi parle-t-on · Les arguments pour · Les risques · Les contre-arguments
      annonce ou fait d'actualité : Ce qui est annoncé · Le contexte · Ce que ça change · Les limites
      étude ou recherche : La question · La méthode · Les résultats · Les réserves
      méthode d'entraînement : Le principe · Ce que dit la science · Comment l'appliquer · Les précautions
      réglementation : Ce qui change · Qui est concerné · Le calendrier · Les points de vigilance
  • « synthese » : 2 phrases (format long) ou 1 à 2 phrases (format court) qui résument l'ensemble.
- Style : français soigné, clair, sans tournures calquées sur l'anglais, sans emphase.
- « republication » : si l'article indique qu'il a été publié initialement à une date antérieure (republication), indique « paru initialement en <mois année> » ; sinon chaîne vide.

Réponds uniquement en JSON, selon cette structure :
{"titre": "…", "chapo": "…", "sections": [{"intertitre": "…", "texte": "…"}], "synthese": "…", "republication": ""}

Format : long
Limite de longueur : 4500 caractères au total.
Édition numérique, lue sur téléphone, sans contrainte de page : la limite suit la matière disponible dans la source. Adapte le nombre de sections à la longueur : 2 sections sous 2 000 caractères, 3 ou 4 jusqu'à 3 500, 4 à 6 au-delà ; même règle de longueur (90 à 100 % de la limite). N'étire jamais une source mince : mieux vaut un article court et exact.
Travail de recherche : utilise EXACTEMENT ces intertitres, dans cet ordre : « La question » (pourquoi ce travail, d'après l'introduction) ; « Les conclusions » (principaux résultats, avec les chiffres) ; « La méthode » (données et démarche, en quelques phrases) ; « Ce que ça implique » (explication accessible des conséquences, telles que les auteurs les présentent) ; « Les limites » (uniquement celles mentionnées par les auteurs ; omets cette section s'ils n'en mentionnent aucune). Remplis « reference » : auteurs, institution ou revue, date, et nature du document (document de travail non relu par des pairs, article de revue à comité de lecture, billet de chercheur…), uniquement d'après le texte fourni.

Unconventional Monetary Policy and Deposit Retention
Philip Strahan and Tuo Yang
NBER Working Paper No. 35985
November 2026
JEL No. E4, G21
ABSTRACT
The two dimensions of unconventional monetary policy — holding the short rate at the zero-lower 
bound (ZLB) and quantitative easing (QE) — shifted deposit composition toward more interest-
sensitive customers. The ZLB drew these customers by creating rate compression, which limited 
the benefit of searching for high-yielding liquidity sources. QE also drew rate-sensitive, large 
depositors from the Federal Reserve’s purchases of bonds from non-banks. Once policy 
normalized, flow sensitivity and the deposit beta both increased with exposure to QE and the ZLB. 
We conclude that unconventional monetary policy made deposit retention costlier and riskier for 
banks.
Philip Strahan
Boston College
Carroll School of Management
and NBER
philip.strahan@bc.edu
Tuo Yang
Boston College
tuo.yang@bc.edu
1 Introduction
Central banks initiated two unconventional monetary policies following the wreck-
age of the Global Financial Crisis (GFC). First, they committed to holding the short-term
policy rate at its zero lower bound for an extended period (ZLB); second, they initiated
Quantitative Easing (QE) to lower long-term rates directly. This paper shows that both
dimensions of unconventional policies shifted the composition of bank deposits toward
more rate-sensitive customers, making it costlier and riskier for banks to retain deposits
once policy normalized.
The ZLB policy led to interest-rate spread compression, both across banks (because
deposit rates collapsed toward zero) and between banks and money markets (because
money market rates also collapsed toward zero). As a consequence, rate-sensitive
liquidity demanders lost the incentive to move funds into high-rate substitutes for
traditional bank deposits, or between banks based on differences in offered interest
rates. This change both increased the flow of overall deposits into banks (see Figures
1 and 2) and also meant that allocation of deposits across banks lost its connection to
deposit rates. As shown in Figure 3, the composition of bank deposits shifted away from
interest-bearing time deposits and toward checkable, non-interest bearing accounts.
This compositional change in deposits, as a consequence of the ZLB, reflects inflows
from interest-sensitive customers, which emerge later when the short rate lifts off zero.
We show that this change in composition affected how deposit supply responded when
monetary conditions normalized.1
QE, or large-scale purchases by the Federal Reserve (“the Fed”) of long-term bonds,
also affected bank financing by mechanically increasing deposits when the bonds sold
originate from outside the banking system (Hancock and Passmore, 2015; Christensen
and Krogstrup, 2019, 2022; Acharya et al., 2024).2 This component of unconventional
1Unlike the Fed, the European Central Bank set its policy rate below zero. This policy created
additional funding problems for banks because they were unable to pass negative rates through fully to
depositors. See Heider, Saidi and Schepens (2019) for a discussion of the policy tradeoffs.
2Deposits created by QE enter into banks, with the reserves created diluting the average risk and
return of their asset portfolios. Banks thus rebalance themselves toward long-term bonds and other risky
assets such as loans, and the portfolio rebalancing activity reaches the wide universe of U.S. banks.
1
monetary policy increased the share of uninsured deposits at banks, as we show, thus
potentially harming funding stability. Uninsured depositors are both more interest-
rate sensitive on average than insured ones, and they also respond to solvency shocks
(because uninsured depositors are exposed to bank failure risk). This latter, latent risk
became manifest during the SVB run and collapse (Jiang et al., 2024; Drechsler et al.,
2026).
We estimate the effects on bank deposits of these two dimensions of unconventional
policy simultaneously, an exercise challenged by the fact that QE, by design, overlaps
with the ZLB. The two policies have different effects on bank stability — one potentially
changes interest-rate sensitivity (the ZLB), while the other affects that and also run
risk by increasing uninsured deposits (QE). But testing their effects separately poses a
challenge because central banks resort to QE only when they have reached the limit of
the standard monetary tool, the short-term money market rate, by putting that rate at
its zero lower bound. Hence, the two policies are inherently coincidental.
We are able to separate the effects of the two policies by exploiting a new instrument
which provides bank-market level variation in exposure to QE, following Yang (2026).
The instrument uses granular data on Fed bond purchases, which are publicly disclosed
at the transaction level. When these bond purchases originate from non-banks, they
mechanically increase deposits at banks, but they are always intermediated at the
original point of sale through a small number of large banks, the so-called Primary
Dealers (PDs). Hence, the initial deposits created are not randomly distributed across
the system. The instrument exploits the fact that non-PD banks with high market
overlap with the PDs experience deposit inflows due to these Fed bond purchases.3
And, the effect on deposits is strongest both statistically and economically for uninsured
deposits. Thus, we can construct a time-varying measure of sensitivity to QE at both
the bank and the bank-county levels.
Our core model relates deposit flows to deposit interest rates, to exposure to QE and
3This measure of QE exposure illustrates the Cantillon Effect, which argues that money creation has
non-neutral effects because it does not reach all economic agents at the same time, as the metaphorical
“helicopter drop” would.
2
its interaction with the deposit rate, and to exposure to ZLB and its interaction with the
deposit rate. Following Begenau and Stafford (2022), we measure the deposit rate using
their construct Rate Gap, which equals the difference between what a given bank pays
for deposits compared to the average amount paid by competing banks raising deposits
in the same local market(s). Rate Gap offers an exogenous (from the local market
perspective) measure of a given bank’s relative aggressiveness in pricing its deposits
because multi-market banks engage almost completely in uniform pricing across local
markets.4 As such, a bank’s relative deposit rate in a given market (compared to
competing banks in that same market) isolates the supply side and does not reflect
local funding demands (which in part drive local deposit growth apart from deposit
rates). We first replicate Begenau and Stafford (2022), who show that Rate Gap strongly
predicts deposit growth at the bank-county-year level (based on deposit growth in the
Summary of Deposits); we then extend their results to show that averaging Rate Gap
up to bank level (across local markets) provides a strong predictor of deposit growth at
the bank-quarter level.
Our model shows that during the ZLB, Rate Gap’s explanatory power for deposits
falls sharply, especially at banks heavily exposed to QE. This happens because spreads
compress toward zero (which is evident in the distribution of deposit rates as well
as in Rate Gap — see Figures 4 and 5), which shifts the composition of deposits from
interest-bearing accounts (especially time deposits) to non-interest bearing ones. Deposit
growth thus loses its connection to interest rates during the ZLB, as differences in rates
are just too small to matter. As such, deposits do not move across banks, and many
new deposits flow into banks generally from money markets because banks provide
marginally higher levels of protection and marginally higher levels of liquidity. Figure
1 shows that bank deposits grow rapidly relative to money market funds during the
ZLB, and the reverse happens outside the ZLB. Said differently, without a pricing edge,
money markets are at a severe competitive disadvantage relative to banks.
4For example, in 2019 the average US bank had over 100 branches but set just 1.1 unique interest rates
across those branches; see Table 1 from Begenau and Stafford (2022).
3
We then test how deposit dynamics change during the two most recent rate cycles,
one after the Global Financial Crisis (GFC) and the other after the Pandemic. Once
interest rates lifted off the ZLB — first in late 2015 and again in 2022 — exposure
to QE increased interest-rate sensitivity of deposit flows. That is, banks with high
QE and ZLB exposure could only retain their deposits by increasing interest rates to
match changes in market conditions. We further show that exposure to both QE and
the ZLB increases bank deposit betas, which measure how aggressively banks raise
deposit rates in response to increasing market rates. Unconventional policy shifted the
composition of bank deposits toward interest-sensitive customers. As a result, when
interest rates increased off the zero lower bound, banks with high exposure to those
policies raised deposit rates more in order to help them retain those deposits, which
otherwise would seek higher yield (either in the money markets or at other banks).
Retaining deposits thus becomes more costly (i.e., higher deposit rates) and riskier (i.e.,
more rate sensitivity) due to banks’ exposure to unconventional policy.
Our paper contributes to several strands of the emerging literature on bank funding
during the post-GFC period.
First, the results speaks to the literature on the deposit franchise value. The seminal
work by Drechsler, Savov and Schnabl (2017) on the deposits channel of monetary policy
emphasizes the sensitivity of bank deposit supply to the spread between money market
rates and bank deposit rates. Banks earn rents on sticky deposits — which generates
the deposit franchise value — because this stickiness allows them to pay below-market
rates. We show that rate sensitivity collapsed from unconventional monetary policy,
leading to large deposit inflows. Despite these inflows, rate compression toward zero
meant that the deposit franchise value was reduced by unconventional monetary policy
(at least on a per-dollar basis). Yet when monetary conditions normalized, exposure
to deposits from unconventional policy eroded the natural interest-rate risk hedge to
offset asset-side losses with value generated by pricing deposits below market rates.5
5Drechsler, Savov and Schnabl (2021) report evidence from this natural hedge, but they do not
consider the two most recent interest rate upcycles where this hedge becomes less effective. Their analysis
ends in 2017.
4
In other words, banks heavily exposed to QE and to the ZLB had to raise deposit rates
in order to keep deposits from flowing out. Consistent with our arguments, Usenko
(2026) shows that interest rate sensitivity is highest among large depositors, exactly
those which we show are drawn into the banking system by unconventional monetary
policies.
Second, we extend Acharya et al. (2024), who argue that QE harmed bank stability
by increasing their exposure to liquidity risk, both in lending and in taking deposits.
They emphasize the asymmetry in liquidity exposure, whereby banks increase liquidity
risk during QE episodes (which is offset by the associated increase in reserves), but do
not lower this exposure when QE ends; this asymmetry results in more fragile banks as
a legacy of the QE programs. Our mechanism focuses on how unconventional policy
— both QE and the ZLB — affected deposit interest sensitivity during rate increasing
periods, which we show increases at banks most exposed to the two components of
unconventional policy.
Third, we contribute to the literature on fragility stemming from the Silicon Valley
Bank (SVB) crisis.6 This literature focuses mainly on SVB’s pathological combination of
long-term assets financed with almost 100 percent uninsured deposits. Jiang et al. (2024)
estimate large duration-related losses at SVB (like many banks) and show that they
had especially high levels of uninsured deposits, which increased fragility. Drechsler
et al. (2026) argue that the deposit franchise itself is fragile because it can support two
equilibria, one in which deposits stay in the bank and the bank earns rents on them
when market interest rates rise (because spreads rise), thus offsetting asset-side losses;
another equilibrium exists, however, in which depositors run under the rational belief
that the bank will become insolvent if other depositors leave. This mechanism neatly
explains the funding problem related to uninsured deposit fragility, but it does not
address the broader effect of deposit composition on interest rate sensitivity, which is the
focus of our paper. Blickle et al. (2025) is closest to our paper, as it shows higher deposit
6Cookson et al. (2026) emphasize the role of social media in amplifying and extending the effects of
the SVB run.
5
flightiness after unconventional policy. However, our paper, unlike theirs, exploits
cross-bank heterogeneity in exposure to both dimensions of unconventional policy. As
such, we can separate the effects of the two components of that policy: the extended
ZLB and large-scale asset purchases from QE.
2 Unconventional Monetary Policy
Monetary stimulus coming out of the Global Financial Crisis, based on reductions
in the short-term interest rate, was viewed as insufficiently powerful to stimulate the
economy and foreclose the possibility of a deflationary spiral like what had occurred
during the 1930s (Friedman and Schwartz, 1963; Bernanke, 1983). In part the problem
emerged from prior declines in interest rates, which had trended down since the middle
of the 1980s and thus reduced the policy space for the Fed to lower interest rates
(Hillenbrand, 2025). As a result, the Federal Reserve dropped its policy rate to near
zero in late 2008, and added two new tools to amplify its influence on overall financial
conditions. First, Forward Guidance was implemented by communicating the Fed’s
intent to leave the short rate at its “Zero Lower Bound” (ZLB) for an extended period
of time. Second, the Fed initiated large-scale asset purchases, aka Quantitative Easing
(QE), designed to put additional downward pressure on long-term interest rates by
buying long-term Treasuries and Mortgage-Backed Securities. The Fed reinstituted both
of these policies in response to the Pandemic.
Bernanke (2017) and Kuttner (2018) survey the policy rationales as well as the em-
pirical evidence about the effectiveness of these unconventional tools. A number of
studies find loosening of financial conditions such as declines in term premia around
policy announcements (e.g., Gagnon et al., 2011; Krishnamurthy et al., 2011; Ehlers, 2012;
Bauer and Neely, 2014) and increases in bank lending for more-exposed banks (Rod-
nyansky and Darmouni, 2017; Luck and Zimmermann, 2020; Chakraborty, Goldstein
and MacKinlay, 2020).7 Neither survey paper, however, considers how these policies
could affect banking stability when monetary conditions normalized.
7Diamond, Jiang and Ma (2024), in contrast, argue that QE constrained lending by filling up bank
balance sheets with reserves and thus displacing balance sheet capacity for lending.
6
We argue that both the persistent use of the ZLB as well as QE could increase
bank exposure to interest-sensitive deposits. Prior to this period, bank deposits had
been largely supplied by sticky customers with low interest elasticity.8 As a result,
deposit spreads increased when interest rates rose; although some deposits did flow
out, the wider spread provided banks with a hedge against losses from holding interest-
sensitive (i.e., long-term) assets like mortgages or mortgage-backed securities. The
utility of this natural hedge could decline with both the persistent ZLB and by QE
because both policies may change the interest sensitivity of bank deposits. Importantly,
this sensitivity only becomes evident when unconventional policy ends and monetary
conditions normalize.
The ZLB changes the composition of bank deposits because it leads to spread com-
pression. As illustrated in Figures 4 and 5, the variation across banks in deposit rates
declines sharply during these periods. Moreover, the difference in rates paid by the
median bank versus that paid by money markets also declines (Figure 6). Hence,
interest-sensitive liquidity demanders, for example corporate CFOs, lose the incentive
to search for yield on their short-term assets. Prior to the ZLB period, many such agents
would park cash in money markets rather than banks to receive higher returns (recall
Figure 1).9 With spread compression, bank deposits become a better option given the
stronger explicit and implicit insurance against losses. This helps explain the rapid
growth of deposits during the years following the GFC, when deposits grew about
twice as fast as nominal GDP (recall Figure 2).
QE as envisioned by Bernanke was tantamount to a swap between private banks
and the Fed of long-term assets for short-term bank reserves. In its basic form, the Fed
would simply purchase a bond from a bank, and pay for that by issuing new reserves
into the selling bank’s Fed account. As such, the selling bank’s liabilities are unaffected,
while its portfolio of assets becomes shorter in duration and higher in liquidity. The
8Argyle et al. (2025) show that high-balance deposits exhibit higher stickiness; Egan et al. (2025) also
show that depositor stickiness varies with deposit size and depositor demographics (age). Lu and Wu
(2026) show that depositor inattention increases stickiness and enhances bank market power.
9The model crashed badly during the week following Lehman Brothers, leading to a government
bailout of the money market industry.
7
policy effect works by moving duration risk from the private banking system to the
government.
The problem with the textbook model of QE, where the Fed’s actions only affect
banks, is that most of the long-term bonds purchased originated outside the banking
system. Carpenter et al. (2015) show, for example, that most of the bonds came from
households (which is a catch-all category from the US Flow of Funds which includes
hedge funds), insurance companies, pension funds, and brokerage firms. None of these
entities can accept reserves from the Fed as payments for bonds sold. Instead, they are
paid in deposits by one of the Primary Dealer banks, which interact directly with the
Fed and act as an intermediary between the original seller and the Fed. The PD banks
then resell the bond to the Fed in return for reserves. The deposits (and reserves) thus
start at one of the PDs but then move to other banks. The new money created by QE
propagates across the banking system gradually, with its largest immediate effects at
banks located near the PD bank locations. Hence, QE in practice is not a simple asset
swap between banks and the Fed; instead, it leads to an expansion of both the asset side
(i.e., more reserves) and the liability side (more deposits) of banks. These new deposits,
as we will show, are not distributed evenly across banks and do not behave similarly to
normal deposits created by private market forces.
3 Data
This section details the data sources used in this paper. Our analysis draws on four
sources. Bank-level financial information comes from the Federal Financial Institutions
Examination Council (FFIEC) Call Reports; branch-level deposit information comes
from the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) Summary of Deposits (SOD)
Data; transaction-level data on the Federal Reserve’s open market operations, used to
construct our QE deposit-channel instrument, come from the Federal Reserve Bank
of New York’s Open Market Operations transaction data; and aggregate macroeco-
nomic time series come from Federal Reserve Economic Data (FRED). The sample
spans 2001 through 2025, covering both the post-financial-crisis and the post-pandemic
8
zero-lower-bound episodes and the tightening cycles that followed each. Detailed
variable definitions and summary statistics are provided in Appendix Tables A.1 and
A.2, respectively.
3.1 FFIEC Call Report Data
Our bank-level analysis uses FFIEC Call Report data accessed through Wharton
Research Data Services (WRDS). This dataset provides comprehensive accounting
information from the Consolidated Reports of Condition and Income, which all insured
commercial banks are required to file each quarter. For each bank-quarter, we retain only
the most recent submission to incorporate amended filings. Because flow variables in
the Call Reports — such as interest expense on deposits — are reported on a year-to-date
basis, we transform them into discrete quarterly flows by subtracting the value from
the preceding quarter within the same fiscal year. From these records, we construct
each bank’s deposits, insured and uninsured deposits, total assets, and its deposit
rate, measured as annualized interest expense on deposits scaled by average deposits.
This yields a consistent quarterly panel of bank balance-sheet and deposit-pricing
outcomes.10
3.2 FDIC Summary of Deposits (SOD) Data
For our local, bank-county analysis we use the FDIC Summary of Deposits (SOD)
data, which provide branch-level deposits and geographic identifiers for all FDIC-
insured institutions. These data are released annually with a reporting date of June
30. We use them to construct, for each bank, the geographic distribution of its deposits
across counties and its deposit market share within each county. Aggregating branch
deposits to the bank-county-year level gives the local deposit measures used throughout
the paper and the predetermined deposit-market weights that underlie our bank-county
analysis.
10When a bank is involved in a merger or failure, we drop the bank-time or bank-county-time
observation which contains the structural change, as this often has a massive effect on rates of change.
9
3.3 FRED Data
We supplement our analysis with aggregate macroeconomic time series from FRED
to characterize the broader economic environment across monetary policy phases. These
series include total deposits at commercial banks, money market mutual fund assets,
nominal GDP, the Federal Funds rate, and the 3-month Treasury bill rate. We use these
data, along with the Federal Funds rate path, to construct our descriptive figures and
date zero-lower-bound episodes.
3.4 Federal Reserve Bond Purchase Data
To construct our core measure of QE’s effect on bank deposits, we use transaction-
level security trade data from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York’s Open Market
Trading Desk. These data record every asset purchase and sale conducted with primary
dealers — the financial institutions authorized to transact directly with the Fed — and
include the trade and settlement dates, transaction type, par and dollar amounts, CUSIP,
and counterparty. Because the Fed’s large-scale asset purchases flowed thro

4.3 Deposit Rate Sensitivity when Monetary Conditions Normalize
Tables 3 through 6 show that deposit-flow sensitivity to the Rate Gap falls during
the ZLB era when QE Exposure is high. In the best-identified models which fully
account for bank-time deposit demand (Tables 5 and 6), the decline in rate sensitivity
happens widely across banks. These patterns suggest that the incremental deposits
flowing into banks are being distorted by unconventional policy. The ZLB, by creating
compression in rates both across banks and between banks and money markets (recall
Figures 4 and 6), may draw in funds from normally rate-sensitive customers who are
putting their liquidity into banks (rather than money markets) for the increased safety
and liquidity. The same argument goes through for deposits pulled into banks by QE.
Once rates move off zero, these deposits start to discriminate more than other deposits
22
based on interest rates. By altering the composition of deposits, both dimensions of
unconventional policy potentially affect how deposit supply responds once rates move
off the zero lower bound.
To test these ideas, we need to capture cross-bank variation in exposure to both QE
and to the ZLB. Unlike QE (where we exploited both county and bank-county variation),
our prior models captured the ZLB with a simple time-series indicator variable. Since
some banks raised more deposits than others during the ZLB quarters, we now exploit
this cross-bank heterogeneity in exposure. We measure this variation using each bank’s
deposit growth accumulated during the ZLB quarters, scaled by assets. To do so, we
build a bank-time-varying ZLB Exposure, defined as the backward-looking, 12-quarter
moving average of the bank’s quarterly deposit change scaled by its total assets at the
start of the ZLB episode, counting only those quarters that occurred during the ZLB
regime (non-ZLB quarters enter as zero). As the moving-average window rolls forward
and ZLB quarters are progressively replaced by non-ZLB quarters, the measure tends
toward zero; because it averages signed deposit changes, however, it need not decline
monotonically. QE Exposure is constructed analogously: it is the 12-quarter moving
average of bank b’s QE-driven deposit inflow, scaled by lagged assets. To ease the
comparisons, we standardize both measures to have zero mean and unit variance.
We estimate the following specification, now using only the data during the two rate
cycles which followed each ZLB episode:
∆Depk b,t/Assetsb,t−1 = β1 Rate Gapb,t + β2 ZLB Exposureb,t−1 + β3 QE Exposureb,t−1
+ β4 Rate Gapb,t × ZLB Exposureb,t−1
+ β5 Rate Gapb,t × QE Exposureb,t−1
+ αr b + γt + ϵb,t
(5)
We estimate this model on the non-ZLB quarters of each episode, so that β1 captures
the rate-gap sensitivity of deposit flows once the policy rate has lifted off its floor,
β4 captures how that sensitivity differs across banks that accumulated more or less
23
deposits during the preceding ZLB episode, and β5 measures the analogous differential
with respect to accumulated QE Exposure. While some of the deposit inflows driving
ZLB Exposure came from QE bond purchases, by controlling for QE Exposure we can
interpret β4 as capturing the marginal effect of the ZLB.26 The specification includes a
separate bank fixed effect for each of the two cycles (αr b) and quarter fixed effects (γt).
The dependent variables ∆Depk b,t are based on total deposits or uninsured deposits. We
cluster standard errors two-way by bank and state-quarter.
A causal reading of this model is complicated by the endogeneity of ZLB Exposure.
Banks choose the amount of deposits raised in response to lending and other investment
opportunities.27 If these (unmeasured) investment opportunities are persistent, they
could affect our estimates of rate sensitivity.
We address this endogeneity concern by replacing each bank’s ZLB Exposure with
predetermined, plausibly exogenous variation in its exposure to the ZLB episode. Our
instrument is a leave-out shift-share measure (Bartik, 1991). As noted above, the ZLB
led to compositional shift away from time deposits and toward non-interest bearing
deposits (recall Figure 3). As such, banks which entered a ZLB era with high levels
of either type would be highly exposed to the policy. To build the measure (ZLB
ExposureBartik b,t ), we compute the national growth rate of each of the three deposit types
(time deposits, savings deposits and non-interest bearing deposits) in every ZLB quarter
(excluding the bank’s own deposits) and then combine these using weights equal to the
bank’s holdings of each deposit type divided by its total assets at the start of the episode.
The resulting predicted inflow is therefore scaled by assets, as is ZLB Exposure, and the
weights sum to the bank’s pre-episode ratio of these deposits to assets rather than to
one. Both the weights and the accumulation window are specific to each episode: in the

5 Conclusion
Both dimensions of unconventional monetary policy, we find, came with the unex-
pected consequence of making deposits both costlier and riskier to retain once policy
normalized. When the Fed decided to lower the short-term policy rate to zero and
committed to leave it there, it did so following a financial crisis sufficiently reminiscent
of the 1930s to make a catastrophic deflationary spiral plausible. Adding additional
monetary stimulus through its large-scale purchase of long-term bonds also seemed
well motivated at the time. But these policies led to very large expansions of bank
deposits from new sources; deposits, for example, grew by 42% between 2010 and 2015
(the first instance of the ZLB), while nominal GDP grew just 26%. These inflows tilted
the composition of bank funding toward more rate-sensitive sources, such as corporate
28
Treasuries which might otherwise park liquidity in the money markets. We exploit
heterogeneity in bank exposure to both QE and the ZLB to show that this composi-
tional change meant that banks had to raise deposits rates more to keep those deposits
once monetary conditions normalized. If future circumstances demand unconventional
responses, policy makers should take into account their effects on bank funding stability.
